Overview

This article covers general troubleshooting steps for database connectivity failures across the organization's supported database platforms: Oracle, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. Use this guide as a first-response reference before escalating to the database administration team.

Common Symptoms

Database connectivity issues typically present as one of the following: application startup failures, intermittent timeouts under load, complete inability to establish a connection, or authentication failures during the connection handshake. The specific error message returned usually points to a distinct root cause category.

Oracle Connection Failures

Oracle connection issues most commonly surface as TNS-related errors. A "could not resolve the connect identifier" error

sues most commonly surface as TNS-related errors. A "could not resolve the connect identifier" error usually indicates a missing or incorrect entry in the tnsnames.ora configuration file, often following a database migration or environment change. Engineers should verify the connect descriptor matches what the DBA team has published for the target environment, and confirm the TNS_ADMIN environment variable points to the correct configuration directory.

PostgreSQL Connection Failures

PostgreSQL connection refusals are frequently caused by network-level restrictions rather than the database itself being down. Two configuration files are the most common culprits: postgresql.conf, which controls which network interfaces the server listens on, and pg_hba.conf, which controls which hosts are permitted to connect and using what authentication method. General Diagnostic Steps

1. Confirm the database service is actually running on the host.
2. Test raw network connectivity to the database port using a tool appropriate to the platform (tnsping for Oracle, psql or telnet for PostgreSQL, sqlcmd for SQL Server).

Knowledge Base Article: Authentication and Access Troubleshooting Guide
Document Type: Knowledge Base
Category: Authentication

Overview

This article covers troubleshooting steps for authentication and access failures, including Active Directory login issues, OAuth token failures, and session-related problems. These issues are among the highest-priority categories since they typically affect many users simultaneously.

Active Directory Login Failures

When newly provisioned users cannot log in,

Active Directory Login Failures

When newly provisioned users cannot log in, the most common cause is that the user account was created but never added to the required security groups that grant access to the target system. Verify group membership directly in Active Directory Users and Computers, and confirm a group policy update has propagated to the affected system - this can take up to 90 minutes by default unless manually forced with gpupdate.

OAuth and Token Exchang

can take up to 90 minutes by default unless manually forced with gpupdate.

OAuth and Token Exchange Failures

An invalid_grant error returned during an OAuth token exchange does not always indicate a credentials problem. One frequently overlooked cause is clock drift: OAuth tokens are time-sensitive, and if the authentication server's system clock has drifted from the reference time source (typically due to a failed NTP synchronization), token validation will fail even though the credentials t

cally due to a failed NTP synchronization), token validation will fail even though the credentials themselves are correct. Always check system time synchronization before investigating credential-related causes.

Session and Token Expiry Issues

Users reporting unexpected logouts or "session expired" errors shortly after logging in should be checked against recent changes to session timeout configuration, load balancer sticky session settings, and clock synchronization across all nodes in a load

uration, load balancer sticky session settings, and clock synchronization across all nodes in a load-balanced authentication cluster. Inconsistent time across nodes can cause tokens issued by one node to appear invalid when validated by another.

Single Sign-On (SSO) Failures

SSO failures are frequently certificate-related. If users are redirected to the identity provider but the redirect back to the application fails, check the certificate used to sign SAML assertions has not expired, and that

the application fails, check the certificate used to sign SAML assertions has not expired, and that the assertion consumer service URL registered with the identity provider matches the application's actual callback URL exactly, including protocol and trailing slashes.

General Diagnostic Steps

1. Confirm whether the issue affects a single user, a group, or the entire organization - the scope strongly indicates whether the cause is account-specific, group-policy-related, or infrastructure-wide.

2. Check system clock synchronization on all authentication infrastructure before deeper investigation, since clock drift is a disproportionately common and easily overlooked root cause.
3. Review recent changes to group policies, identity provider configuration, or certificate renewals.
4. Reproduce the exact error message, since generic "cannot log in" reports often map to several unrelated roo

Escalation

If the issue affects more than a handful of users or appears infrastructure-wide, escalate immediately to the identity and access management team rather than troubleshooting individual accounts.
